title: US Credit Card Debt Climbs to $1.26 Trillion as Auto Loans Hit Record
excerpt: The New York Fed's Q2 2026 household debt report shows credit card balances rising again toward record territory, while auto loan originations reached an all-time nominal high of $211 billion.
body:
• US credit card debt rose to $1.26 trillion in Q2 2026, approaching the all-time record of $1.28 trillion set in Q4 2025.
  • Auto loan originations hit a record $211 billion in the quarter, though the figure is not adjusted for inflation.
  • Overall delinquency rates fell in Q2, but credit card serious delinquency remains elevated at around 12.8%, up from 7.6% in late 2022.
  • Home equity borrowing rose by $19 billion as homeowners avoid refinancing at current high mortgage rates.

US consumers pushed credit card balances back toward record levels in the second quarter while taking out a record amount in auto loans, according to the Federal Reserve Bank of New York's latest household debt and credit report released Tuesday.

Credit card debt climbed to $1.26 trillion in the April-June period, reversing the seasonal decline that brought balances down to $1.25 trillion in Q1 and edging closer to the all-time record of $1.28 trillion reached at the end of 2025.

Auto Loans Break Records

Auto loan originations reached $211 billion in Q2, a nominal record, though Fed researchers noted the figure is not adjusted for inflation. A pandemic-era surge in auto purchases in 2021 also produced quarterly borrowing near $200 billion but was accompanied by sharply higher vehicle prices.

Home equity line of credit balances rose by $19 billion, continuing a four-year trend that Fed researchers attribute to older homeowners tapping existing equity rather than refinancing their mortgages at today's elevated rates.

Overall consumer debt fell slightly to $18.8 trillion in Q2, though the decline was linked to a change in how mortgage data is reported. The New York Fed expects the drop in mortgage debt recorded in Q2 to be offset by a corresponding increase in the next report.

Delinquencies: Stabilizing but Elevated

The overall delinquency rate fell in the second quarter, a signal that household balance sheets on average remain resilient despite declining inflation-adjusted incomes.

Credit card delinquencies, however, tell a more nuanced story. While the pace at which borrowers fall behind on payments has been unchanged for roughly two years, the accumulated effect has been significant. The share of credit card debt more than 90 days past due climbed from 7.6% in late 2022 to 12.8% at the start of this year.

"Credit card spending still appears solid, and while delinquency rates are elevated compared to the pre-pandemic period, they appear to have stabilized."

— New York Fed staff economists

In an accompanying blog post, New York Fed economists said a closer look at the delinquency data shows the pace of deterioration has plateaued, even though the stock of troubled debt remains high.

The K-Shaped Consumer Economy

The data reinforces what economists have called a K-shaped consumer economy. Higher-income households are maintaining spending and paying down balances, while lower-income borrowers face compounding pressure from elevated interest rates.

The average credit card APR now exceeds 21%, according to Federal Reserve data. At that rate, a $6,500 revolving balance — close to the national average — generates roughly $114 in monthly interest charges. Minimum payments on balances of that size barely cover the interest, leaving principal nearly untouched and stretching payoff timelines across years.

Earlier data from the Philadelphia Fed found that the share of credit card accounts paying only the minimum balance has declined to 10.24%, retreating from a record high of more than 11% at the end of 2024. At the same time, the share of accounts paid in full has increased — evidence that the consumer divide is widening rather than the typical cardholder simply doing better.

Looking Ahead

The Q2 data arrives amid ongoing uncertainty about the trajectory of interest rates and consumer spending. With credit card debt climbing back toward record levels and auto borrowing at nominal highs, the resilience of the US consumer will continue to be tested — particularly for households on the wrong side of the K.
nri_angle: Rising consumer debt and elevated interest rates affect household finances across the US, with the data carrying implications for spending, savings, and investment decisions.
